The standard route is a long, non-technical Class 2 scree/talus ascent via the Wolf Creek Trail and Gardner Meadows, almost always done as a 2–3 day backpack rather than a day trip. This rout

overview: Alpine gully route up Guye Peak's south side: climbs a chockstone-choked gully, then exits onto the South Spur for the final push to the summit. Popular moderate objective near Snoqualmie Pass, climbed as a summer/fall scramble and, under snow, in winter.

The North Ridge starts in the deep notch just north of the fin and climbs about seven pitches on or just west of the crest to the summit. overview: Hozomeen Mountain is a dramatic, dark twin-summited peak rising directly from the east shore of Ross Lake near the Canadian border in North Cascades National Park/Ross Lake National Recreation Area. The higher North Peak (~8,071-8,072 ft) and slightly lower South Peak (8,003 ft) are built of Hozomeen chert, a hard but badly fractured bedded rock that gives the mountain its dark color and its reputation for notoriously loose, rotten climbing. The South Peak's nearly 1,000-foot near-vertical face
beta: Mostly Class 3-4 scrambling on loose, fractured rock above the 6,800 ft saddle camp: slabs and connecting gullies lead up the south side to a slanted ledge below the summit, where a short, exposed wall of about 15 ft at roughly 5.6 is the crux, followed by a chimney finish. Most parties rappel the crux on the way down. Previous climbing experience on exposed, loose rock is essential.

overview: La Bohn Peak (6,585 ft) is a granite summit at the head of Necklace Valley in the eastern Alpine Lakes Wilderness, rising directly west of La Bohn Gap — a broad, tarn-dotted saddle around 5,900 ft between the peak and Mount Hinman (7,492 ft, 1.7 mi east). The standard line follows a climbers' path west from the gap up the ridge and face above La Bohn Lakes, gaining a final ~1,000 ft of Class 2 (occasional Class 3) talus and rock to the summit. It's rarely climbed on its own — most parties tag it
beta: From a camp at La Bohn Lakes or La Bohn Gap, climbers head west from the gap up boulders and heather onto the east ridge. Parties describe crossing to a false summit just short of the true top, with roughly the final 1/8 mile being a walk along the summit ridge. The line is entirely off-trail Class 2-3 talus with no technical climbing required in summer conditions.

overview: Little Tahoma Peak (11,138 ft) is the third-highest summit in Washington and the most prominent remnant of the much larger, older Mount Rainier edifice that has since eroded away, standing as a jagged andesite pyramid on Rainier's east flank above the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers. First climbed August 29, 1894 by J.B. Flett and Henry Garrison via this same east-shoulder line from Summerland. The rock is shattered, hydrothermally altered andesite, and the peak is chronically unstable — a Decemb
beta: Approach from Summerland alpine meadow via the Fryingpan Glacier, aiming southwest toward Whitman Crest notch at 9,000 feet. Cross the Whitman Glacier and ascend to the summit block, where a short but serious Class 4 scramble (30-40 feet) on loose andesite reaches the true summit. The route is graded as a moderate alpine climb, feasible for competent glacier climbers but not for beginners.
